newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin takes over in unemotional handover.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin takes over in unemotional handover.

text.p: The challenge for France's brand-new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Tuesday morning was to look serious. For conservative Alain Juppe, the defeated premier, it was to keep a smile on his face.
Jospin was positively beaming as he walked out of his new Matignon offices for the first time after taking power, escorting Juppe to a waiting car.
He had to suck in his lips to wipe the broad smile off his face and take on a more dignified look.
Juppe clearly had to force a grin as he waved respectfully to the crowd of dignitaries and journalists before ducking into the car and speeding off.
The event, from Jospin's arrival to Juppe's swift departure, unrolled in less than a quarter of an hour and with little pomp.
Apart from the colourful Republican Guards and the red carpet on the stairway leading into Matignon, there was no public ceremony, only handshakes and cursory waves to onlookers.
Jospin moved in to Matignon after leading his leftist alliance to a stunning upset win over the ruling centre-right in Sunday's National Assembly election runoff.

Juppe, humiliated in defeat, faced an uncertain future as crippled leader of the Gaullist Rally for the Republic party (RPR), senior partner in the former government. Party grandees have lost no time in blaming Juppe personally for the defeat and in staking their own claims to the succession.

President Jacques Chirac, the RPR's founder, called the snap election nearly a year ahead of schedule in hopes of renewing his huge centre-right majority for another five years and giving France a "new elan" to carry it into European monetary union.
His gamble went horribly wrong, and the centre-right was instead dumped from power.
After Monday's formal handover, which took place behind closed doors, Juppe said the occasion had gone "quite well".
His former chief aide Maurice Gourdault-Montagne, who witnessed the transfer of power, said it had been businesslike and unemotional.
"It was very republican, very tidy. Democracy continues," he told Reuters afterwards.

As Juppe prepared to leave, the Matignon kitchen crew -- more than a dozen men in white uniforms including some wearing tall chefs' caps, looked on discreetly from the side of the courtyard, perhaps wondering how the changeover would affect their own futures.
Was a special luncheon planned for Jospin? "We don't know," ventured one of the chefs.
Will Jospin actually live at Matignon, as had Juppe after being forced out of his luxury rent-controlled Paris flat in a housing scandal? "We know nothing at all," the chef responded.
Afterwards, in the courtyard, it became clear who in the crowd had been among the winners and who were among the losers.
Winners pulled out portable telephones and strode briskly for the gate, checking on their next appointments.
Losers held back, saying their goodbyes and giving the simple but dignified courtyard a final weary inspection, as if to fix it in their memories.
"What will you do?" a woman asked Gourdault-Montagne.
"I don't know," he said, shrugging his shoulders.
